claim: Eukaryotes and prokaryotes last shared a common ancestor approximately 2 billion years ago.
source: Eukaryotes and prokaryotes last shared a common ancestor ~2 billion years ago
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established scientific consensus about the timing of divergence between eukaryotes and prokaryotes.

claim: 31 out of 51 bacterial genes tested (61%) could complement a lethal growth defect and replace their yeast orthologs after accounting for mitochondrial localization and alternative start codons.
source: After accounting for mitochondrial localization and alternative start codons, 31 out of 51 bacterial genes tested (61%) could complement a lethal growth defect and replace their yeast orthologs with minimal effects on growth rate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study, specifically shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Replaceability was determined on a pathway-by-pathway basis.
source: Replaceability was determined on a pathway-by-pathway basis; codon usage, abundance, and sequence similarity contributed predictive power.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the computational analysis of features predicting replaceability, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The heme biosynthesis pathway was particularly amenable to inter-kingdom exchange, with each yeast enzyme replaceable by its bacterial, human, or plant ortholog.
source: The heme biosynthesis pathway was particularly amenable to inter-kingdom exchange, with each yeast enzyme replaceable by its bacterial, human, or plant ortholog, suggesting it as a near-universally swappable pathway.
evidence: This is a major finding from the experimental data on heme pathway genes, as shown in Figures 4, 6, and 7.

claim: Eukaryotes and prokaryotes share hundreds of genes.
source: Despite over 2 billion years of divergence, eukaryotes and prokaryotes still share hundreds of genes (Theobald, 2010; O'Brien et al., 2005; Brown and Doolittle, 1997; Martin and Müller, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Yeast and E. coli share 58 genes that are essential in yeast and have clear 1:1 orthologs in either species.
source: Yeast and E. coli share hundreds of genes, 58 of which are essential in yeast and have clear 1:1 orthologs in either species.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A, representing the starting dataset for the study.

claim: 51 of 58 E. coli genes provided informative assays for replaceability in yeast.
source: 51 of these 58 E. coli genes provided informative assays for replaceability in yeast.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 25 of 51 E. coli genes (~49%) could functionally replace their orthologous yeast counterparts in initial complementation assays.
source: Initial results from these complementation assays revealed that 25 of 51 (~49%) E. coli genes could functionally replace their orthologous yeast counterparts.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A, representing the initial screening results.

claim: Haploid yeast gene deletion strains carrying plasmids expressing functionally replacing E. coli genes generally exhibit comparable growth rates to the wild type parental yeast strain BY4741.
source: Haploid yeast gene deletion strains carrying plasmids expressing functionally replacing E. coli genes (red solid-lines) generally exhibit comparable growth rates to the wild type parental yeast strain BY4741 (black dotted-lines).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C with growth curve data.

claim: 15 of the 51 tested E. coli genes have mitochondrially-localized yeast orthologs.
source: Many eukaryotic orthologs of prokaryotic genes function in specific subcellular compartments absent from prokaryotes, and consistent with this trend, 15 of the 51 tested E. coli genes have mitochondrially-localized yeast orthologs (Cherry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to the yeast database.

claim: All but one of the 15 E. coli genes with mitochondrially-localized yeast orthologs were unable to replace their yeast ortholog.
source: Because all but one of these 15 genes were unable to replace their yeast ortholog, we reasoned that lack of mitochondria targeting might account for their failed complementation.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Four E. coli genes could functionally replace their yeast equivalents after adding a mitochondrial localization signal.
source: We added the mitochondrial localization signal (MLS) from the yeast MIP1 gene to each of the 14 non-replaceable E. coli genes and repeated the complementation assays. Four genes could now functionally replace their yeast equivalents (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: EGFP-tagged Ec-MLS-HscB and Ec-MLS-IlvD proteins correctly traffic to yeast mitochondria.
source: We verified mitochondrial localization by fusing the E. coli Ec-MLS-HscB and Ec-MLS-IlvD proteins with enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) and confirming correct trafficking of the EGFP-tagged proteins to yeast mitochondria (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C with microscopy images.

claim: Approximately 14% of all E. coli ORFs employ an alternative start codon.
source: Bacterial genes also occasionally lack a standard ATG start codon, with ~14% of all E. coli ORFs employing an alternative start codon (Blattner et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the E. coli genome paper.

claim: Two E. coli genes (Ec-rcsC and Ec-tadA) could replace their yeast orthologs after changing their start codons to ATG.
source: After changing their start codons to ATG, two of these four E. coli genes, Ec-rcsC and Ec-tadA, could now replace their yeast orthologs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In one-fifth of the cases, replaceability depended on proper subcellular localization or start codon choice.
source: In one-fifth of the cases, replaceability depended on proper subcellular localization or start codon choice to express the prokaryotic gene in the proper eukaryotic context.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data showing 6 out of 31 replaceable genes required these modifications.

claim: Protein sequence similarity between orthologs was not a highly predictive feature of replaceability.
source: Notably, the extent of protein sequence similarity between orthologs was not a highly predictive feature.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A and 3B with computational analysis.

claim: The three most divergent orthologs that replaced each showed less than 20% amino acid sequence identity.
source: A large portion of the tested E. coli and yeast orthologs showed only 20–30% identical amino acid sequences and roughly half of these genes were replaceable; in contrast, the three most divergent orthologs replaced, each showing less than 20% identity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fraction of interaction partners that replace was the most predictive property tested for replaceability.
source: Having a high fraction of interaction partners that replace was the most predictive property tested, suggesting that the ability to replace is a modular phenomenon whereby genes functioning together are similarly able to replace.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A with AUC analysis.

claim: A Random Forest classifier constructed with all attributes achieved an AUC of 0.79 for predicting replaceability.
source: Combining all of these features into a single predictor (after accounting for mitochondrial localization and alternative start codons), using a random forest classifier, improved our predictive power to a 0.79 AUC (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Different biological processes displayed varied replaceability, with metabolic processes being largely replaceable while processes like ribosomal processing were much less replaceable.
source: Consequently, different biological processes (as defined by GO) displayed varied replaceability, with metabolic processes being largely replaceable, while processes known to be divergent, including ribosomal processing, were much less replaceable (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C with GO category analysis.

claim: Most of the enzymatic reactions in the heme biosynthesis pathway are identical between E. coli and yeast.
source: Most of the enzymatic reactions in the heme biosynthesis pathway are identical between E. coli and yeast, but there are clear differences in the way this pathway functions between the species (Heinemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation.

claim: Yeast condenses succinyl-CoA and glycine to produce delta-aminolevulinate in a single enzymatic step catalyzed by Sc-Hem1.
source: Yeast condense succinyl-CoA and glycine to produce delta-aminolevulinate in a single enzymatic step catalyzed by Sc-Hem1
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the yeast heme pathway.

claim: E. coli produces delta-aminolevulinate in two steps using glutamyl-tRNA as a precursor.
source: while E. coli produces delta-aminolevulinate in two steps using glutamyl-tRNA as a precursor (Yin and Bauer, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation describing the E. coli heme pathway.

claim: The bacterial heme pathway is largely cytosolic but in yeast it is partitioned between the mitochondria and cytosol.
source: Second, the bacterial heme pathway is largely cytosolic but in yeast it is partitioned between the mitochondria and cytosol (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Co-expression of E. coli Ec-HemA and Ec-HemL successfully replaced yeast Sc-HEM1 gene function.
source: Co-expression of the two E. coli genes successfully replaced yeast gene function (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: E. coli Ec-HemD and Ec-HemG are not orthologs of yeast genes but carry out identical reactions to Sc-Hem4 and Sc-Hem14, respectively.
source: Additionally, two enzymes, Ec-HemD and Ec-HemG, were not identified as orthologs between E. coli and yeast, despite carrying out identical reactions to Sc-Hem4 and Sc-Hem14, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing non-orthologous gene displacement.

claim: Non-orthologous E. coli genes Ec-HemD and Ec-HemG successfully replaced their functionally analogous yeast genes.
source: Expression of these non-orthologous but functionally analogous E. coli genes in the respective yeast deletion strains showed that they were indeed able to successfully replace the yeast genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Sc-Hem14 and Sc-Hem15 carry out the final two steps in yeast heme biosynthesis and are localized to the mitochondria.
source: Sc-Hem14 and Sc-Hem15 carry out the final two steps in yeast heme biosynthesis and are localized to the mitochondria (Cherry et al., 2012; Koh et al, 2015) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: E. coli Ec-HemG and Ec-HemH are both predicted to localize to the plasma membrane in E. coli.
source: As E. coli lack mitochondria, and Ec-HemG and Ec-HemH are both predicted to localize to the plasma membrane in E. coli (Papanastasiou et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation.

claim: E. coli Ec-HemG and Ec-HemH localized to the yeast plasma membrane when expressed as EGFP-fusion proteins.
source: Strikingly, both localized to the yeast plasma membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 with microscopy images.

claim: Concurrent bacterialization of both yeast genes Sc-HEM14 and Sc-HEM15 resulted in a viable but defective yeast strain.
source: However, concurrent bacterialization of both yeast genes resulted in a viable but defective yeast strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: All CRISPR-edited heme biosynthesis pathway strains but two grew comparably to wild-type yeast.
source: All strains but two grew comparably to the wild-type; the Sc-hem14∆::Ec-hemG and Sc-hem15∆::Ec-hemH strains showed modest growth defects (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B with growth curves.

claim: Addition of the yeast MLS to Ec-hemG and Ec-hemH completely ameliorated growth defects from the ORFs alone.
source: The addition of the yeast MLS to each E. coli ORF completely ameliorated growth defects from the ORFs alone (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Sc-hem15Δ::Ec-hemH yeast strain turned pink on standard YPD agar medium upon prolonged incubation of 3–4 days.
source: In the course of constructing the CRISPR-edited yeast strains, we noticed that the Sc-hem15∆::Ec-hemH yeast strain turned pink on a standard YPD agar medium upon prolonged incubation of 3–4 days (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The pink phenotype was consistent across all independently obtained, sequence verified yeast clones of Sc-hem15Δ::Ec-hemH.
source: This phenotype was consistent across all independently obtained, sequence verified yeast clones.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a control for the phenotype observation.

claim: The pink phenotype decreased dramatically in the Sc-hem15Δ::Ec-MLS-hemH strains where Ec-HemH was correctly localized to the mitochondria.
source: The pink phenotype decreased dramatically in the Sc-hem15∆::Ec-MLS-hemH strains in which Ec-HemH was correctly localized to the mitochondria by addition of an MLS.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The pink pigment from Sc-hem15Δ::Ec-hemH corresponds to protoporphyrin IX.
source: Therefore, we chemically extracted the pink pigment from Sc-hem15∆::Ec-hemH, Sc-hem15∆::Ec-MLS-hemH and wild type yeast cells (Materials and methods) and performed fluorescence spectroscopy to determine that the pigment likely corresponds to protoporphyrin IX (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with spectroscopy data.

claim: Several clones of the Sc-ΔMLS-HEM15 yeast strain displayed similar extracellular pigment to Sc-hem15Δ::Ec-hemH.
source: In order to determine whether protein mis-localization contributed to the phenotype, we removed the MLS from the native yeast gene. Several clones of the Sc-ΔMLS-HEM15 yeast strain displayed similar extracellular pigment (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Sc-hem15Δ::Ec-HemH hem14Δ strain lost the pink phenotype.
source: Consistent with protoporphyrin IX being the pink pigment in the Sc-hem15Δ::Ec-HemH strain, the Sc-hem15Δ::Ec-HemH hem14Δ strain lost the pink phenotype, even after growing for 6 days.
evidence: This is stated in the text as experimental evidence supporting the identity of the pigment.

claim: All strains carrying the hem14Δ allele were significantly paler than wild type BY4741 cells.
source: Moreover, we observed that all strains carrying the hem14Δ allele were in fact significantly paler than even wild type BY4741 cells, presumably reflecting extensive protoporphyrin IX depletion in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In humans, disrupting heme biosynthesis leads to the disease porphyria.
source: In humans, disrupting heme biosynthesis leads to the disease porphyria, and the secretion of porphyrin intermediates is specifically observed in a subtype known as protoporphyria (Bloomer et al., 1998)
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation.

claim: Reduced activity of the human heme pathway protein Hs-FECH leads to accumulation and subsequent secretion of protoporphyrin IX into surrounding tissues in protoporphyria.
source: wherein reduced activity of the human heme pathway protein Hs-FECH leads to accumulation and subsequent secretion of protoporphyrin IX into surrounding tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the human disease.

claim: The first enzymatic step in the plant heme biosynthetic pathway is similar to bacteria, a two-step reaction using glutamyl-tRNA as a substrate.
source: The first enzymatic step in the plant heme biosynthetic pathway is similar to bacteria, a two-step reaction using glutamyl-tRNA as a substrate (Figure 6A and B) (Ilag et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Co-expression of plant genes At-HEMA1 and At-GSA2 functionally replaced the corresponding yeast gene function.
source: We expressed both plant genes, At-HEMA1 and At-GSA2, simultaneously and were able to functionally replace the corresponding yeast gene function.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an experimental result.

claim: Neither At-HEMA1 nor At-GSA2, when individually expressed, could functionally replace the yeast gene.
source: Neither protein, when individually expressed, could functionally replace the yeast gene (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In Arabidopsis, a majority of genes in the heme biosynthesis pathway have acquired lineage-specific amplifications, resulting in two co-orthologs for each single yeast gene.
source: In Arabidopsis, unlike for the case of E. coli, a majority of genes in the heme biosynthesis pathway have acquired lineage-specific amplifications, resulting in two co-orthologs for each single yeast gene (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All Arabidopsis co-orthologs replaced successfully except one case where only one replaced (At-CPX1 replaced while At-CPX2 did not), and one case where neither replaced (At-HEME1 and At-HEME2).
source: In these cases, we tested both co-orthologs individually for replaceability; all replaced successfully, with the exception of one case where only one replaced (At-CPX1 replaced while At-CPX2 did not), and one case where neither replaced (At-HEME1 and At-HEME2) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,B''').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B and supplementary figures.

claim: Both Arabidopsis paralogs At-PPOX1 and At-PPOX2 could efficiently complement the yeast gene Sc-HEM14.
source: Both Arabidopsis paralogs that we tested, At-PPOX1 and At-PPOX2, could efficiently complement the yeast gene responsible for this critical step, Sc-HEM14 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The single soybean ortholog Gm-HEMG successfully complemented the Sc-hem14 deletion growth defect.
source: As for each of the Arabidopsis paralogs, the single soybean ortholog also successfully complemented the Sc-hem14 deletion growth defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B'.

claim: EGFP fusions of At-PPOX1 and At-FC1 showed clear mitochondrial localization in yeast.
source: EGFP fusions of At-PPOX1 and At-FC1 showed clear mitochondrial localization in yeast (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A with microscopy images.

claim: Plant chloroplast localization signals appear to be recognized and processed as mitochondrial localization signals in yeast.
source: Thus, these plant chloroplast localization signals appear to be recognized and processed as mitochondrial localization signals in yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization data of plant proteins in yeast.

claim: Removing the chloroplast localization signal from At-HEMC markedly enhanced its ability to functionally replace its yeast ortholog.
source: We found that removing the chloroplast localization signal (CLS) from At-HEMC markedly enhanced its ability to functionally replace its yeast ortholog (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B''.

claim: Neither of two Arabidopsis paralogs, At-HEME1 and At-HEME2, could functionally replace their yeast ortholog, Sc-HEM12, even after removing their CLS sequences or when co-expressed.
source: In contrast, neither of two Arabidopsis paralogs, At-HEME1 and At-HEME2, could functionally replace their yeast ortholog, Sc-HEM12, even after removing their CLS sequences, or even when co-expressed in the yeast strain (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B''').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B'''.

claim: Human Hs-ALAD, Hs-HMBS, Hs-CPOX and Hs-FECH have been shown to successfully replace yeast heme biosynthesis genes in earlier studies.
source: Earlier studies have shown successful replacement of the yeast heme biosynthesis genes by their human orthologs Hs-ALAD (Schauer and Mattoon, 1990), Hs-HMBS, Hs-CPOX and Hs-FECH (Kachroo et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior studies.

claim: Hs-UROS expression resulted in toxicity in earlier studies.
source: while Hs-UROS expression resulted in toxicity and Hs-UROD failed to replace its yeast ortholog (Kachroo et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior studies.

claim: Toxicity from Hs-UROS could be abrogated by inserting the human gene at the native yeast chromosomal locus.
source: In the case of Hs-UROS, we reasoned that toxicity was due to expression from the heterologous constitutive promoter (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A). Indeed, similar to the results obtained with the yeast version of this gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Sc-HEM4), we found that toxicity could be abrogated by inserting the human gene at the native yeast chromosomal locus, thus providing native yeast gene expression and regulation for the human ORF (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: The human ORFeome clone of Hs-UROD contained a mutation (G303V) that when reverted to wild-type sequence allowed it to replace the yeast gene.
source: We also found that the human ORFeome clone of Hs-UROD contained a mutation (G303V) that when reverted to wild-type sequence allowed it to replace the yeast gene (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C and D)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: Human Hs-PPOX could complement the severe growth defect of the yeast Sc-hem14 deletion strain.
source: and we additionally confirmed that human Hs-PPOX could complement the severe growth defect of the yeast Sc-hem14 deletion strain (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In humans, the initial step of heme biosynthesis is identical to that of yeast (Sc-HEM1) but is encoded by two co-orthologs, Hs-ALAS1 and Hs-ALAS2.
source: Finally, in humans, the initial step of heme biosynthesis is identical to that of yeast (Sc-HEM1) but is encoded by two co-orthologs, Hs-ALAS1 and Hs-ALAS2.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the human heme pathway.

claim: Both human genes Hs-ALAS1 and Hs-ALAS2 could individually replace the yeast gene function.
source: We found that both of these human genes could individually replace the yeast gene function (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The last three proteins in the human heme biosynthesis pathway are mitochondrially localized.
source: The subcellular localization of heme biosynthesis differs slightly between humans and yeast, such that the last three proteins in the human heme biosynthesis pathway are mitochondrially localized, as opposed to only the last two in yeast (Grandchamp et al., 1978; Ferreira et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations.

claim: EGFP-tagged Hs-FECH, Hs-PPOX, and Hs-CPOX all localized to mitochondria in yeast.
source: Indeed, EGFP-tagged Hs-FECH, Hs-PPOX, and Hs-CPOX all localized to mitochondria in yeast (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B with microscopy images.

claim: The human mitochondrial localization signal is recognizable by the yeast localization machinery.
source: confirming that the human mitochondrial localization signal is recognizable by the yeast localization machinery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization data of human proteins in yeast.

claim: During eukaryogenesis, early eukaryotes adopted a large portion of the bacteria-like heme biosynthesis pathway of their endosymbiont mitochondria.
source: During eukaryogenesis, early eukaryotes adopted a large portion of the bacteria-like heme biosynthesis pathway of their endosymbiont mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the evolutionary history of the heme pathway.

claim: The subsequent endosymbiotic acquisition of chloroplasts along the plant lineage resulted in redundancy between mitochondrial-origin and chloroplast-origin portions of their heme biosynthesis pathways.
source: The subsequent endosymbiotic acquisition of chloroplasts along the plant lineage (Oborník and Green, 2005) resulted in redundancy between mitochondrial-origin and chloroplast-origin portions of their heme biosynthesis pathways, a state that can be observed today in Euglena, a non-plant, photosynthetic eukaryote with more recently acquired chloroplasts (Kořený and Oborník, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations describing the evolutionary history.

claim: Over time, plants kept the chloroplastic system and lost most of the mitochondrial system of heme biosynthesis.
source: Over time, plants kept the chloroplastic system and lost most of the mitochondrial system.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the evolutionary history of the plant heme pathway.

claim: Heme biosynthesis genes are freely exchangeable between bacteria, plants (with the exception of At-HEME), humans, and yeast.
source: Taking these data together with literature studies showing successful replacement of the E. coli Ec-hemG gene by the plant or human Hs-PPOX gene (Lermontova et al., 1997; Dailey and Dailey, 1996; Narita et al., 1996), and that introducing the protoporphyrinogen oxidase from Bacillus subtilis into plants improves yields (Lee et al., 2000), heme biosynthesis thus appears to be a pathway whose genes are freely exchangeable between bacteria, plants (with the exception of At-HEME), humans, and yeast (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a major conclusion stated in the text with citations to supporting literature and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Approximately 61% (31/51) of the tested E. coli and yeast genes still retain ancestral function to a sufficient extent that the bacterial genes efficiently replace their yeast equivalents.
source: We discovered that ~61% (31/51) of the tested E. coli and yeast genes still retain ancestral function to a sufficient extent that the bacterial genes efficiently replace their yeast equivalents.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding from the study.

claim: Eukaryote-specific features such as subcellular localization (4 of 14) and proper start codon usage (2 of 4) were critical for swappability for some of the E. coli orthologs.
source: Eukaryote-specific features such as subcellular localization (4 of 14) and proper start codon usage (2 of 4) were critical for swappability for some of the E. coli orthologs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings from the study.

claim: Amino acid sequence similarity was not the most important property for predicting replaceability.
source: Our analysis of replaceable/non-replaceable orthologous pairs revealed that amino acid sequence similarity was not the most important property, consistent with a general trend for sequence conservation to often more strongly reflect other attributes of protein function (e.g., abundance and protein-specific functional constraints) (Jordan et al., 2002; Wang and Zhang, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The top predictors of replaceability were features attributed to specific gene modules.
source: Rather, the top predictors of replaceability were features attributed to specific gene modules.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational analysis of replaceability predictors.

claim: Functional replaceability is predominantly determined at the level of pathways and processes, even across very large evolutionary distances.
source: These results largely agree with previously published work on humanization of yeast genes (Kachroo et al., 2015; Hamza et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2016), suggesting that functional replaceability is predominantly determined at the level of pathways and processes, even across very large evolutionary distances.
evidence: This is a major conclusion stated in the text with citations to supporting studies.

claim: Metabolism-associated genes replace more often than those involved in 'informational' processes like transcription or translation.
source: As our assays can be considered a form of forced horizontal gene transfer, our results provide support for the 'complexity hypothesis' (Jain et al., 1999), which posits that informational (transcription, translation, etc.) genes are less likely to be horizontally transferred than those genes that are operational (metabolism, housekeeping, etc.). Consistent with this expectation, we see metabolism-associated genes replacing more often than those involved in 'informational' processes like transcription or translation.
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and supported by the data on GO category replaceability.

claim: Orthologous genes carry out similar functions that allow for their ability to functionally replace each other across even the 2 billion year evolutionary rift separating prokaryotes and eukaryotes from their last common ancestor.
source: Our results thus demonstrate that orthologous genes carry out similar functions that allow for their ability to functionally replace each other across even the 2 billion year evolutionary rift separating prokaryotes and eukaryotes from their last common ancestor.
evidence: This is a major conclusion stated in the text summarizing the findings.

claim: Yeast and humans are relatively similar – both eukaryotes that share thousands of genes and the majority of their core biological processes.
source: However, in the timescale of evolution, yeast and humans are relatively similar – both eukaryotes that share thousands of genes and the majority of their core biological processes.
evidence: This is stated in the text as background context.

claim: The ability of human genes to functionally replace their yeast orthologs is not strongly predicted by the similarity of sequences, but rather at the level of specific pathways or processes.
source: The ability of human genes to functionally replace their yeast orthologs is not strongly predicted by the similarity of sequences, but rather at the level of specific pathways or processes, wherein all genes in a process or pathway tend to be similarly replaceable, or not (Kachroo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to prior work.

claim: Data on eukaryote – prokaryote functional gene replacement are sparse.
source: Data on eukaryote – prokaryote functional gene replacement are sparse (Heinicke et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation, providing motivation for the study.

claim: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic orthologs diverged significantly at the amino acid sequence level.
source: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic orthologs also diverged significantly at the amino acid sequence level (O'Brien et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation.

claim: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic orthologs evolved distinct expression patterns and codon usages.
source: and evolved distinct expression patterns and codon usages (Sharp et al., 1993; Bulmer, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations.

claim: Eukaryotes and bacteria are known to use many of the same orthologs to perform the same metabolic enzymatic reactions.
source: Nonetheless, eukaryotes and bacteria are known to use many of the same orthologs to perform the same metabolic enzymatic reactions (Jardine et al., 2002; Peregrin-Alvarez et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations.

claim: The ortholog-function conjecture forms the basis of most modern biomedical research and is widely used to predict new gene function across organisms.
source: This conjecture forms the basis of most modern biomedical research and is widely used to predict new gene function across organisms (Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation.

claim: Several large-scale studies have confirmed that many human orthologs can successfully replace their yeast counterparts.
source: There are many individual examples of genes from one species functioning for their orthologous counterparts in a different species (Cherry et al., 2012; Heinicke et al., 2007), but this trend has only recently begun to be explored systematically, with several large-scale studies substituting human genes for yeast genes and confirming that many human orthologs can successfully replace their yeast counterparts (Kachroo et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2016; Hamza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior studies.

claim: At the level of evolutionary divergence of yeast and humans, data demonstrate widespread functional conservation, even after 1 billion years of divergence.
source: At the level of evolutionary divergence of yeast and humans, such data demonstrate widespread functional conservation, even after 1 billion years of divergence.
evidence: This is stated in the text summarizing prior findings.

claim: Plasmid-borne copies of yeast genes complemented their corresponding heterozygous diploid deletion alleles at a high rate (100% for 29 strains tested).
source: We have previously demonstrated that plasmid-borne copies of yeast genes complemented their corresponding heterozygous diploid deletion alleles at a high rate (100% for 29 strains tested in Kachroo et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to prior work as a control.

claim: Six yeast genes were able to complement the growth defect when expressed on a CEN plasmid under the control of the constitutive GPD promoter.
